quote: Which classification of B cannot be ruled out from this figure alone?
source: transcript 9/28 (~57%): "if I give you that figure in the right, you can't differentiate between a competitive and an inverse because you're at 0 and there's no change." The item has no graph object; his version is a figure question (Pharmacodynamics reviews.pdf page 9: one dotted/solid pair, one shift right).
fix: Add graph:{curves:[{label:'A alone', ec:-0.5, emax:100, dashed:true}, {label:'A + B', ec:0.7, emax:100}], base:0, x:'log dose agonist', y:'% of maximal response'} and keep the stem; or, if no figure, change 'from this figure alone' to 'from this description alone'.

quote: Both lower the Emax, which is unchanged here.
source: transcript 9/28 (~94%): "I didn't give you enough shifts, could this be irreversible? Maybe"; transcript 9/30 (review page 9, one shift right): "could it be either one of those three? All I gave you is one shift ... Could I get some shift before I see that drop happening? Yes" and "could this be an allosteric antagonist that affects only affinity? That's another option". With one shift and spare receptors he does not rule the irreversible antagonist out.
fix: An allosteric antagonist affecting efficacy always lowers the Emax, so this pair is out; the irreversible antagonist is only excluded once enough shifts are drawn without a drop (spare receptors can delay it).

quote: A second full agonist also shifts left, but it has efficacy of its own, so each pretreatment dose would raise the baseline; here the baseline never moves.
source: Pharmacodynamics reviews.pdf page 8 and transcript 9/30: dotted curve to the left, same top, baseline 0 — "the baseline changing? No ... two possible answers. It's either full agonist. Or an allosteric agonist that affecting what, affinity." He keyed BOTH full agonist and allosteric agonist on a left shift with no baseline change, and separated allosteric from orthosteric by symmetry (page 10: "if you see a figure in your exam that the shifts are not symmetric, you already know it's allosteric").
fix: A second full agonist also shifts left, but as an orthosteric drug its shifts would be symmetrical and keep going; here the shifts are unequal and stop growing, which is allosteric.

quote: a partial agonist can only bring the response to its own efficacy, so the curves would not all finish at 100% from wherever they start.
source: none found — the 9/28 FA + PA example (dopamine/aripiprazole, ~37%) is the partial agonist added to a system at 100% ("bring that baseline to about 60%"); he never drew a full agonist's DRC rebuilt after partial-agonist pretreatment, and by mass action the full agonist still outcompetes a reversible partial agonist at high dose.
fix: Albuterol is a partial agonist: it would raise the baseline only to its own efficacy and, competing for the pocket, make norepinephrine's life harder rather than easier; a baseline climbing toward 100% with a left shift is two full agonists.

quote: Albuterol is a partial agonist; alone it rises from the 50% baseline toward its own plateau below 100%.
source: transcript 9/30 (review page 4, same figure): "Could it be a partial agonist who has efficacy of 50%? So it doesn't matter if he's bound or unbound, he's doing whatever the system is doing ... Could you say with certainty that C was a partial agonist? ... Yes [with a second cell line] ... You can't say on the one on the left, if I don't give you more information. It's a competitive based on the information that I gave you." He accepts that a 50%-efficacy partial agonist is also flat at 50 on this figure; only the 'based on the information given' rule keys metoprolol.
fix: Albuterol is a partial agonist; alone it goes up or down from the 50% baseline to its own efficacy. (A partial agonist with exactly 50% efficacy would also sit flat, but with no more information a flat line is read as the competitive antagonist.)
